content: A dodecahedron is a polyhedron that consists of twelve faces. Typically, when referring to a dodecahedron, one means the regular dodecahedron, which is a Platonic solid composed of twelve regular pentagonal faces. At each vertex, three faces meet. This geometric structure has twenty vertices and thirty edges. Its dual polyhedron is the icosahedron. In ancient Greek philosophy, the dodecahedron symbolized the universe. Among the Platonic solids, if all are constructed with edges of the same length, the dodecahedron would be the largest. The surface area (A) and volume (V) of a regular dodecahedron with edge length (a) can be calculated using specific mathematical formulas. The Cartesian coordinates of its vertices, when centered at the origin, are defined using the golden ratio ((phi = frac{1 + sqrt{5}}{2})). The side length of the dodecahedron is (2 / phi = sqrt{5} 1), and the radius of the sphere that contains the dodecahedron is approximately (sqrt{3}). The regular dodecahedron is the third in an infinite series of truncated trapezohedra, which can be constructed by truncating the two axial vertices of a pentagonal trapezohedron. Its stellations form three of the four Kepler-Poinsot polyhedra. A rectified dodecahedron results in an icosidodecahedron. The regular dodecahedron has 120 symmetries, forming the group (A_5 times Z_2). The vertex arrangement of the dodecahedron is shared with four non-convex uniform polyhedra and three uniform compounds. Five cubes can fit within a dodecahedron, with their edges acting as diagonals of the dodecahedron's faces. Together, these form the regular polyhedral compound of five cubes. Additionally, two tetrahedra can fit on alternate cube vertices, allowing five or ten tetrahedra to also fit within a dodecahedron. The term dodecahedron is also used to describe other polyhedra with twelve faces. Notably, the rhombic dodecahedron, which is dual to the cuboctahedron (an Archimedean solid), occurs naturally as a crystal form. To distinguish it, the Platonic solid dodecahedron is sometimes called a pentagonal dodecahedron or a regular dodecahedron. The pyritohedron is an irregular pentagonal dodecahedron. Other dodecahedra include various uniform polyhedra, such as the pentagonal antiprism (10 equilateral triangles and 2 pentagons) and the decagonal prism (10 squares and 2 decagons). Johnson solids, such as the pentagonal cupola (5 triangles, 5 squares, 1 pentagon, and 1 decagon), snub disphenoid (12 triangles), elongated square dipyramid (8 triangles and 4 squares), and metabidiminished icosahedron (10 triangles and 2 pentagons), also fall into this category. Congruent non-regular faced dodecahedra include the hexagonal bipyramid (12 isosceles triangles, dual of the hexagonal prism), hexagonal trapezohedron (12 kites, dual of the hexagonal antiprism), triakis tetrahedron (12 isosceles triangles, dual of the truncated tetrahedron), and the rhombic dodecahedron (12 rhombi, dual of the cuboctahedron). Other non-regular faced examples include the hendecagonal pyramid (11 isosceles triangles and 1 hendecagon), trapezo-rhombic dodecahedron (6 rhombi and 6 trapezoids, dual of the triangular orthobicupola), and the rhombo-hexagonal dodecahedron or elongated dodecahedron (8 rhombi and 4 equilateral hexagons). Artifacts resembling dodecahedra have been discovered in various locations across Europe, though their purpose remains uncertain. A dodecahedron appears in M.C. Escher's lithograph Reptiles (1943), and a stellated dodecahedron is featured in his work Gravitation. Salvador Dalí incorporated a hollow dodecahedron into the room design of his painting The Sacrament of the Last Supper (1955). In the children’s novel The Phantom Tollbooth (1961), a character named Dodecahedron is depicted as a man with twelve faces. In the Doctor Who episode Meglos (1980), a dodecahedron serves as the mysterious power source for an underground city. In The Simpsons episode Blood Feud, Lisa attempts to teach Maggie the word dodecahedron. In Carl Sagan's novel Contact, the transport device constructed according to alien plans is dodecahedral in shape. The term dodecahedron also appears in popular culture, such as in a song by Aphex Twin, albeit misspelled as dodecaheedron. The dodecahedron has been associated with philosophical and scientific ideas. Plato linked the Platonic solids to the four classical elements, while Aristotle added a fifth element, aether, which he associated with the heavens but did not explicitly connect to the dodecahedron. In 2003, Jean-Pierre Luminet and colleagues suggested that the shape of the universe might be a finite dodecahedron, connected to itself by opposite faces to form a Poincaré homology sphere. However, subsequent astronomical searches for evidence supporting this hypothesis yielded no results. The dodecahedron has also appeared in early computer games. Its 20 vertices and 30 edges formed the map for the game Hunt the Wumpus. In the 1980s game Elite, advanced Dodec class space stations were shaped like dodecahedra. Save points in the Castlevania games Symphony of the Night and Harmony of Dissonance are dodecahedral. In the Nintendo 64 game Paper Mario, the mountains in the background of Toad Town are shaped like dodecahedra. The regular dodecahedron is commonly used in role-playing games as a twelve-sided die (referred to as d12). Occasionally, desk calendars are designed in the shape of a dodecahedron, typically made from die-cut folded card, with one month displayed on each face.
